rules.title: Good-cause eviction protections for New Jersey residential tenants
rules.requirement: A residential landlord generally may evict or refuse to renew only for statutory good cause and through the court eviction process. Most causes require a written Notice to Quit, and some also require a prior Notice to Cease; notice periods vary by cause.

coverage.other_unresolvable: Does not apply to transient or seasonal hotel, motel, or guest-house occupants, except hotel and motel occupants with no alternate residence who reside there continually; does not apply to a unit held in trust for an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies the unit.
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rental properties, including single-family homes, mobile homes and mobile-home park land, apartment buildings and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes.

rules.exemptions: May not apply to two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; does not apply to transient or seasonal hotel, motel, or guest-house rentals; does not apply to certain units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member.
rules.interaction: For eviction based on nonpayment of a rent increase, the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord must have good cause to evict a tenant (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53). There are several grounds for a good cause eviction.

rules.title: Unconscionable rent increases cannot support eviction
rules.requirement: A landlord may seek eviction for failure to pay a rent increase only if the tenant received notice and a Notice to Quit, and the increase is not unconscionable. A tenant who believes an increase is unconscionable may withhold the difference between the old rent and the new rent for a court to decide.
rules.key_value: rent increase must not be unconscionable

coverage.other_unresolvable: Same Anti-Eviction Act coverage limitations: transient or seasonal hotel, motel, or guest-house occupants are excluded, except continuous hotel or motel residents with no alternate residence; certain trust-held units for developmentally disabled immediate family members are excluded.
coverage.summary: Applies within the Anti-Eviction Act’s coverage of most New Jersey residential rental properties.

rules.exemptions: Same Anti-Eviction Act exceptions, including possible exclusion for two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units and transient or seasonal guest housing.
rules.interaction: The document states that the rent increase must also comply with municipal ordinances, including rent control.
rules.quoted_span: The rent increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control.

rules.title: Ban on self-help evictions and lockouts
rules.requirement: A landlord may not remove a tenant, lock a tenant out, shut off utilities to force a tenant out, or hold the tenant’s belongings without a court order or the tenant’s consent. Only a court officer may physically evict a tenant after a judge issues a warrant for removal.

coverage.summary: Applies to occupied rental premises and dwelling units in New Jersey as described in the document.

rules.penalty: A tenant who is illegally evicted may seek possession and damages; in a successful forcible-entry-and-detainer action, the court may award possession, all damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney fees. The landlord may also be charged with disorderly conduct if they refuse re-entry after police warning.
rules.interaction: This rule works with the eviction process by requiring a judgment and warrant before physical removal; it does not state any local preemption.
rules.quoted_span: Self-help evictions, or lockouts, made by the landlord are illegal in New Jersey.
